name: Anti-consumerism
scope: Anti-consumerism as the sources define it: a social ideology that decries excessive purchasing and consumption of material goods, above all goods bought for novelty, status or manufactured needs, and the resource depletion, debt, conspicuous consumption, inequality and global poverty it is held to produce (Britannica); in the scholarship, a movement of consumers, activists and subvertisers who reject or reduce consumption and resist advertising (Makri, Lekakis, Humphery's 'new politics of consumption': culture jamming, simple living, slow food, fair trade). It is a cultural and ethical critique more than a full political programme; narrowly religious asceticism and wholesale primitivism are outside it unless the sources tie them in.

sources.title: Excess: Anti-consumerism in the West (Humphery, Polity 2010; publisher description, Wiley-VCH)

summary: Anti-consumerism is a social ideology that decries excessive buying and consuming of material goods, especially for novelty, status or manufactured needs, and the resource depletion, debt, inequality and poverty it is held to cause. Scholarship treats it as a movement of consumers and activists (culture jamming, simple living, slow food, fair trade) that resists advertising and consumer culture. It is a cultural and ethical critique, so its defining sources state a position on very few of the test's statements.
